items.title: Lattice paths, step sets and step words
items.strategy: Fix a finite $S\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^2$, the **step set**. A **lattice path of length $n$ with steps in $S$ from $P$ to $Q$** is a function $v:\{0,1,\dots,n\}\to\mathbb{Z}^2$ with $v(0)=P$, $v(n)=Q$ and $v(i)-v(i-1)\in S$ for $1\le i\le n$. Its **step word** is the word $w\in S^n$ with $w_{i-1}=v(i)-v(i-1)$, using the word vocabulary of [[def-finite-words-factor-avoidance-and-prefix-states]] with alphabet $S$. Define concatenation of paths (translate the second so its start meets the first's end) and the empty path. STATE THE $n=0$ CASE EXPLICITLY: the unique path of length $0$ from $P$ is $v(0)=P$, its step word is the empty word, and it is a path from $P$ to $P$. Do not define "the" lattice path graph or any geometry: a path here is a finite point sequence and nothing else, because no topology of the plane is available at this order.

items.title: For each start point the step word is a bijection onto $S^n$
items.strategy: For fixed $P$ and $n$, the map sending a path to its step word is a bijection from the set of length-$n$ paths starting at $P$ onto the set of words of length $n$ over $S$; the inverse takes $w$ to the partial-sum function $v(i)=P+\sum_{j<i}w_j$. Hence that set is finite of size $\lvert S\rvert^{n}$ ([[thm-cardinality-of-a-set-of-functions]], with $\lvert S^n\rvert=\lvert S\rvert^n$ in $\mathbb{N}$). Check $n=0$: one path, one word, $\lvert S\rvert^0=1$, including when $S=\varnothing$. Exhibit a two-sided inverse rather than arguing injectivity and surjectivity separately ([[thm-a-function-is-a-bijection-exactly-when-it-has-a-two-sided-inverse]]).

items.title: Monotone lattice paths with steps $E=(1,0)$ and $N=(0,1)$
items.strategy: The special case $S=\{E,N\}$ with $E=(1,0)$ and $N=(0,1)$; write $\mathcal{M}(P,Q)$ for the set of monotone paths from $P$ to $Q$. Record that a monotone path from $(a,b)$ to $(c,d)$ exists exactly when $c\ge a$ and $d\ge b$, and that it then has length $(c-a)+(d-b)$, so the length is determined by the endpoints. Both degenerate cases ($c=a$, or $d=b$, or both) are named.

items.title: $\lvert\mathcal{M}((0,0),(m,n))\rvert=\binom{m+n}{n}$
items.strategy: Send a path to the set of positions in $\{0,\dots,m+n-1\}$ carrying an $N$ step. This is a bijection from $\mathcal{M}((0,0),(m,n))$ onto the $n$-element subsets of an $(m+n)$-element set, whose count is $\binom{m+n}{n}$ by [[def-binomial-coefficient]]. Give the inverse explicitly (a subset determines the step word). Check $m=n=0$: one path, $\binom{0}{0}=1$; and $n=0$: one path, $\binom{m}{0}=1$. Translation invariance gives the count from $(a,b)$ to $(c,d)$ as $\binom{(c-a)+(d-b)}{d-b}$ and should be a stated clause, since every later count uses it.

items.title: Diagonal lattice paths with steps $U=(1,1)$ and $D=(1,-1)$, and the height function
items.strategy: The step set $\{U,D\}$ with $U=(1,1)$, $D=(1,-1)$. A diagonal path of length $n$ from $(0,a)$ has $v(i)=(i,h(i))$ for a function $h:\{0,\dots,n\}\to\mathbb{Z}$ with $h(0)=a$ and $h(i)-h(i-1)\in\{1,-1\}$; call $h$ the **height function** and prove that $h$ determines the path. Say **touches the level $c$** for $h(i)=c$ for some $i$. Fix once and for all that a diagonal path from $(0,a)$ to $(n,b)$ exists exactly when $n\ge0$, $\lvert b-a\rvert\le n$ and $n\equiv b-a\pmod 2$.

items.title: The two step sets describe the same objects: $U\mapsto N$, $D\mapsto E$ is a bijection matching the diagonal $y=x$ with the level $0$
items.strategy: THE DICTIONARY ITEM, and it is required rather than optional: the page uses both pictures and must say once, with proof, that they agree. Send the diagonal path from $(0,0)$ with $u$ up-steps and $d$ down-steps to the monotone path from $(0,0)$ to $(d,u)$ obtained by replacing each $U$ by $N$ and each $D$ by $E$. Prove this is a bijection from diagonal paths of length $u+d$ ending at $(u+d,u-d)$ onto $\mathcal{M}((0,0),(d,u))$, and prove the boundary correspondence: after $i$ steps the diagonal height is $h(i)$ and the monotone position is $(x_i,y_i)$ with $h(i)=y_i-x_i$, so **$h(i)\ge c$ holds exactly when $y_i-x_i\ge c$**. In particular height $\ge0$ corresponds to staying weakly above the diagonal $y=x$. Do not assert the correspondence anywhere else on the page; cite this lemma.

items.title: The number of diagonal paths from $(0,a)$ to $(n,b)$ is $\binom{n}{(n+b-a)/2}$ when $n\equiv b-a\pmod2$ and $\lvert b-a\rvert\le n$, and $0$ otherwise
items.strategy: Translate to start at $(0,0)$, apply the dictionary lemma and the rectangle count. Solve $u+d=n$, $u-d=b-a$ for $u=(n+b-a)/2$; the parity and range conditions are exactly solvability of that system in $\mathbb{N}$, and the "otherwise $0$" clause must be proved, not assumed, since later differences of counts rely on the vanishing.

items.title: A diagonal path with $h(0)\le c\le h(n)$ or $h(n)\le c\le h(0)$ satisfies $h(i)=c$ for some $i$
items.strategy: The discrete intermediate-value step, and the whole content of the reflection argument. Induct on $n$, or take the least $i$ with $h(i)\ge c$ and use $h(i)-h(i-1)=\pm1$ to force $h(i)=c$. Steps change height by exactly one, which is where $\{U,D\}$ is used and where a larger step set fails; the companion page's counterexample points here.

items.title: Reflecting the initial segment at the first visit to level $c$
items.strategy: Let $a>c$ and $b>c$. For a diagonal path $h$ from $(0,a)$ to $(n,b)$ that touches level $c$, let $\tau$ be the least $i$ with $h(i)=c$ and set $(\rho h)(i)=2c-h(i)$ for $i\le\tau$ and $(\rho h)(i)=h(i)$ for $i\ge\tau$. Prove: $\rho h$ is a diagonal path from $(0,2c-a)$ to $(n,b)$ (the two clauses agree at $i=\tau$, and a reflected step is again a step); $\rho$ maps into paths from $(0,2c-a)$ and every such path touches $c$ by [[lem-a-diagonal-path-that-changes-side-of-a-level-meets-it]] since $2c-a<c<b$; and $\rho$ applied twice is the identity, because the first visit to $c$ is at the same index for $h$ and $\rho h$. A TWO-SIDED INVERSE IS THE PROOF: do not argue "reflect and count".

items.title: The reflection principle: paths from $(0,a)$ to $(n,b)$ staying strictly above level $c$ are counted by a difference of two binomial coefficients
items.strategy: Let $a>c$ and $b>c$. By [[lem-reflection-at-the-first-visit-to-a-level-is-a-bijection]] the paths from $(0,a)$ to $(n,b)$ that touch $c$ are equinumerous with all paths from $(0,2c-a)$ to $(n,b)$. Subtract from the total, using [[thm-sum-rule]] on the disjoint split into touching and non-touching paths, and read both totals off [[cor-diagonal-lattice-paths-with-a-prescribed-endpoint-are-counted-by-a-binomial-coefficient]]. Keep the whole computation in $\mathbb{N}$ by stating it as "touching $+$ avoiding $=$ total" and deriving the difference form only where subtraction is legitimate. Landmark. Attribute the argument to André's method as reported by Krattenthaler §10.3 and Renault; the statement is Krattenthaler Theorem 10.3.1 in the diagonal picture.

items.title: Bertrand's ballot problem: for $p>q\ge0$ the orderings in which the first candidate is strictly ahead throughout satisfy $(p+q)\,N=(p-q)\binom{p+q}{p}$
items.strategy: Model an ordering as a diagonal path from $(0,0)$ of length $p+q$ with $p$ up-steps ending at height $p-q$, and "strictly ahead after every vote" as $h(i)\ge1$ for $1\le i\le p+q$. The first step is forced to be $U$, so $N$ is the number of paths from $(1,1)$ to $(p+q,p-q)$ with $h\ge1$ throughout, i.e. strictly above level $0$. Apply [[thm-reflection-principle-for-diagonal-lattice-paths]] with $a=1$, $b=p-q$, $c=0$ to get $N=\binom{p+q-1}{p-1}-\binom{p+q-1}{p}$, then clear denominators with [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]] to reach the STATED $\mathbb{N}$-IDENTITY $(p+q)N=(p-q)\binom{p+q}{p}$ rather than the quotient form; give the quotient $\frac{p-q}{p+q}\binom{p+q}{p}$ as a second clause computed in $\mathbb{R}$. Check $q=0$ (both sides give $N=1$) and $q=p-1$. Landmark.

items.title: The weak ballot count: for $p\ge q\ge0$ the orderings in which the first candidate is never behind satisfy $(p+1)\,N=(p-q+1)\binom{p+q}{q}$
items.strategy: Prepend one extra up-step: a path of length $p+q$ from $(0,0)$ with $p$ up-steps and $h(i)\ge0$ throughout corresponds bijectively to a path of length $p+q+1$ from $(0,0)$ with $p+1$ up-steps and $h(i)\ge1$ for $i\ge1$. Apply [[thm-ballot-problem]] with $(p+1,q)$ in place of $(p,q)$ and simplify. Exhibit the bijection; do not assert it. Check $p=q$, which is the case the Catalan development uses, and $q=0$.

items.title: Dyck paths of semilength $n$
items.strategy: A **Dyck path of semilength $n$** is a diagonal path from $(0,0)$ to $(2n,0)$ whose height function satisfies $h(i)\ge0$ for every $i$. Write $\mathcal{D}_n$ for the set of them. State the $n=0$ case: the empty path is the unique Dyck path of semilength $0$, so $\mathcal{D}_0$ has one element; $\mathcal{D}_1=\{UD\}$. Define a **ballot word** as the step word of a Dyck path, i.e. a word in $\{U,D\}^{2n}$ with equally many $U$s and $D$s in which every prefix has at least as many $U$s as $D$s, and record that step words identify $\mathcal{D}_n$ with the set of ballot words of length $2n$. Landmark.

items.title: $\mathcal{D}_n$ is a finite set
items.strategy: THE WELL-DEFINEDNESS OBLIGATION FOR THE CATALAN NUMBERS. $\mathcal{D}_n$ injects into the set of words of length $2n$ over $\{U,D\}$ by [[lem-lattice-paths-are-determined-by-their-step-words]], that set is finite of size $2^{2n}$, and a subset of a finite set is finite ([[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]]). Therefore $\lvert\mathcal{D}_n\rvert$ is a well-defined natural number. Nonempty because $(UD)^n\in\mathcal{D}_n$, which also gives $\lvert\mathcal{D}_n\rvert\ge1$ for every $n$ including $n=0$.

items.title: The Catalan number $C_n:=\lvert\mathcal{D}_n\rvert$
items.strategy: DEFINE $C_n$ AS A COUNT, never by a formula: $C_n:=\lvert\mathcal{D}_n\rvert\in\mathbb{N}$, well defined by [[lem-dyck-paths-of-a-given-semilength-form-a-finite-set]] (list that lemma in \`justified_by\`, not in \`deps\`). Record $C_0=1$ and $C_1=1$ from the definition. A Remark fixes the indexing convention against the sources: $C_n$ counts semilength-$n$ Dyck paths, equivalently ballot words of length $2n$, so $C_0=1$; this is the convention of Krattenthaler §10.3 and Stanley. Landmark. Every closed formula on this page is a THEOREM about this count.

items.title: $C_n+\binom{2n}{n+1}=\binom{2n}{n}$
items.strategy: A Dyck path of semilength $n$ is exactly a diagonal path from $(0,0)$ to $(2n,0)$ that never touches level $-1$: heights are integers, so $h(i)\ge0$ fails somewhere exactly when $h(i)=-1$ somewhere, by [[lem-a-diagonal-path-that-changes-side-of-a-level-meets-it]]. Apply [[thm-reflection-principle-for-diagonal-lattice-paths]] with $a=b=0$, $c=-1$: the paths that DO touch $-1$ are equinumerous with all paths from $(0,-2)$ to $(2n,0)$, of which there are $\binom{2n}{n+1}$. State the result in the additive $\mathbb{N}$ form displayed in the title so no subtraction is needed; the difference form $C_n=\binom{2n}{n}-\binom{2n}{n+1}$ is a second clause. Verify $n=0,1,2,3$ against $1,1,2,5$. Landmark.

items.title: $(n+1)\,C_n=\binom{2n}{n}$
items.strategy: From [[thm-catalan-numbers-by-reflection]] it suffices to prove $(n+1)\binom{2n}{n+1}=n\binom{2n}{n}$, which follows from [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]] by clearing factorials in $\mathbb{N}$: both sides times $(n+1)!\,(n-1)!$ equal $(n+1)\,(2n)!$ for $n\ge1$, and $n=0$ is checked directly. STATE THE IDENTITY MULTIPLICATIVELY, in $\mathbb{N}$; give $C_n=\binom{2n}{n}/(n+1)$ only as a second clause about the corresponding computation in $\mathbb{R}$, and do not write the canonical embedding applied to a natural number anywhere. Landmark.

items.title: $n+1$ divides $\binom{2n}{n}$ for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$
items.strategy: Immediate from [[cor-catalan-closed-formula]]: $\binom{2n}{n}=(n+1)C_n$ with $C_n\in\mathbb{N}$, which is exactly divisibility in the sense of [[def-divides-in-z]]. The point worth making in a Remark is that the divisibility is proved by exhibiting the quotient as a COUNT, so no arithmetic argument is needed; this is what the companion page's false statement is refuted by.

items.title: Cyclic shifts of an integer word and its periodic partial-sum function
items.strategy: For $m\ge1$ and a word $a=a_0\cdots a_{m-1}$ of integers, define the **weight** $\lVert a\rVert=\sum_{i<m}a_i$ and, for $j\in\mathbb{Z}$, the **shift** $(\sigma^j a)_i=a_{(i+j)\bmod m}$. Define the **periodic partial-sum function** $S_a:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}$ EXPLICITLY, by $S_a(qm+r)=q\lVert a\rVert+\sum_{i<r}a_i$ for the unique $q\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $0\le r<m$ given by division with remainder; prove from that formula the two facts everything below uses, $S_a(j)-S_a(j-1)=a_{(j-1)\bmod m}$ and $S_a(j+m)=S_a(j)+\lVert a\rVert$. Defining $S_a$ on $\mathbb{Z}$ by a closed formula avoids any two-sided sequence machinery, which the library does not have.

items.title: Cyclic shifting is an action of $\mathbb{Z}/m$ on the words of length $m$ over a set
items.strategy: Check $\sigma^0=\mathrm{id}$ and $\sigma^{j}\sigma^{k}=\sigma^{j+k}$, and that $\sigma^j$ depends only on $j$ modulo $m$, so the additive group of [[def-integers-modulo-n]] acts in the sense of [[def-group-action]]. Also record that shifting preserves the multiset of letters, hence the weight, so the shift acts on the set of words with a prescribed number of each letter.

items.title: If $\gcd(\lVert a\rVert,m)=1$ then the shift stabiliser of $a$ is trivial, so its orbit has exactly $m$ elements
items.strategy: Suppose $\sigma^d a=a$ with $0\le d<m$ and put $g=\gcd(d,m)$. Then $\sigma^g a=a$ by [[thm-bezout-identity]] (write $g=xd+ym$), so $a$ is $g$-periodic and $\lVert a\rVert=(m/g)\,t$ where $t$ is the sum of one period. Hence $m/g$ divides both $\lVert a\rVert$ and $m$, so it divides $\gcd(\lVert a\rVert,m)=1$ and $g=m$, forcing $d=0$. The orbit size is then $m$ by [[thm-orbit-stabilizer]] together with Lagrange's index count. The hypothesis is exactly what the Catalan application supplies, where the weight is $1$.

items.title: $\sigma^{j}a$ has all partial sums positive exactly when $S_a(i)>S_a(j)$ for every $i>j$
items.strategy: First show the partial sums of $\sigma^j a$ are $S_a(j+r)-S_a(j)$ for $1\le r\le m$, directly from the difference identity of [[def-cyclic-shift-and-the-periodic-partial-sum-function]]. So all of them are positive exactly when $S_a(i)>S_a(j)$ for $j<i\le j+m$. Then upgrade "for one period" to "for all $i>j$" using $S_a(i+m)=S_a(i)+\lVert a\rVert$ and $\lVert a\rVert\ge1$, by induction on how many periods $i$ lies beyond $j$. Call an index $j$ with $S_a(i)>S_a(j)$ for all $i>j$ a **strict right minimum**.

items.title: If every $a_i\le1$ and $\lVert a\rVert\ge1$, the strict right minima form a two-sided increasing list on which $S_a$ increases by exactly $1$ at each successive index
items.strategy: Three separate claims, each a numbered block. (i) EXISTENCE: for every integer $M$ the set $\{i:S_a(i)\le M\}$ is nonempty and bounded above, because $S_a(i)\to\pm\infty$ along $i\mapsto i\pm m$ by $S_a(i+m)=S_a(i)+\lVert a\rVert$ with $\lVert a\rVert\ge1$; its greatest element $j$ (which exists by [[lem-int-bounded-above-has-greatest]]) is a strict right minimum. (ii) VALUE: for that $j$, $S_a(j+1)>M\ge S_a(j)$ and $S_a(j+1)\le S_a(j)+1$ because every $a_i\le1$; hence $S_a(j)=M$ exactly when $M$ is attained, and in general $S_a(j)=M$ whenever the set is defined by that $M$ and $M$ is a value of $S_a$. State (ii) as: for each integer $M$ in the range of $S_a$ there is exactly one strict right minimum $j$ with $S_a(j)=M$. (iii) SUCCESSION: consecutive strict right minima have $S_a$-values differing by exactly $1$, so $j\mapsto j+m$ carries a strict right minimum to one exactly $\lVert a\rVert$ places further along the list. THE HYPOTHESIS $a_i\le1$ IS USED ONLY IN (ii) AND IS INDISPENSABLE; say so, since it is the hypothesis a reader will drop.

items.title: The cycle lemma (Dvoretzky–Motzkin): if every $a_i\le1$ and $\lVert a\rVert=k\ge1$, then exactly $k$ of the $m$ cyclic shifts of $a$ have all partial sums positive
items.strategy: Combine [[lem-cyclic-shift-positivity-is-a-strict-right-minimum-of-the-partial-sums]] and [[lem-strict-right-minima-of-a-quasiperiodic-partial-sum-function]]: the good shifts correspond to the strict right minima in $\{0,1,\dots,m-1\}$, and by the succession clause each window of $m$ consecutive integers contains exactly $k$ of them. State the box-and-circle special case of Dershowitz–Zaks §1 ($m$ boxes of value $1$ and $n$ circles of value $-\mu$, giving $m-\mu n$ good shifts) as a clause, since that is the form the applications use and the form the sources state. FIX THE ORIENTATION CONVENTION HERE, in one sentence, and cite it everywhere: a shift is counted when ALL its partial sums are STRICTLY POSITIVE, and shifts are indexed so that $\sigma^{j}a$ begins at position $j$. Sources disagree about which end is cut; a page that mixes conventions gets the bijection pointing the wrong way. Landmark.

items.title: $(2n+1)\,C_n=\binom{2n+1}{n}$, a second derivation of the Catalan count
items.strategy: A GENUINELY DIFFERENT ROUTE from [[thm-catalan-numbers-by-reflection]]: a group action replaces the reflection bijection. Let $W$ be the set of words of length $2n+1$ over $\{+1,-1\}$ with exactly $n$ entries $-1$; then $\lvert W\rvert=\binom{2n+1}{n}$ and every $a\in W$ has $\lVert a\rVert=1$, so [[thm-cycle-lemma]] gives exactly one good shift per word and [[lem-a-word-whose-weight-is-coprime-to-its-length-has-a-trivial-shift-stabiliser]] gives every orbit exactly $2n+1$ elements. The orbits partition $W$ ([[thm-orbits-partition-the-set]]), so $\lvert W\rvert=(2n+1)\cdot(\text{number of orbits})$ and the number of good words equals the number of orbits. Finally, deleting the forced leading $+1$ is a bijection from good words onto ballot words of length $2n$, hence onto $\mathcal{D}_n$. Conclude $(2n+1)C_n=\binom{2n+1}{n}$, and record the agreement with [[cor-catalan-closed-formula]] as a numbered step, since $(2n+1)^{-1}\binom{2n+1}{n}=(n+1)^{-1}\binom{2n}{n}$ is an identity that must be proved, not observed. Landmark.

items.title: If $\lVert a\rVert=1$ then $j\mapsto\#\{r:0\le r<m,\ S_a(j+r)\le S_a(j)\}$ is a bijection from $\{0,\dots,m-1\}$ onto $\{1,\dots,m\}$
items.strategy: THE REFINEMENT OF THE CYCLE LEMMA THAT CHUNG–FELLER NEEDS, and the reason [[thm-cycle-lemma]] does not already give it: the cycle lemma counts the shifts all of whose partial sums are positive, while this lemma sorts EVERY shift by how many of its partial sums are nonpositive. Source: Huq, *Generalized Chung-Feller Theorems for Lattice Paths*, Theorem 2.1.1, whose rational perturbation $S_a(i)-i/m$ is replaced here by the integer key it clears to, so nothing leaves $\mathbb{Z}$. Write $X(j)=\#\{r:0\le r<m,\ S_a(j+r)\le S_a(j)\}$; the case $r=0$ always qualifies, so $X(j)\ge1$. Numbered steps. (1) Put $T(i)=m\,S_a(i)-i$ for $i\in\mathbb{Z}$. From $S_a(i+m)=S_a(i)+\lVert a\rVert=S_a(i)+1$ ([[def-cyclic-shift-and-the-periodic-partial-sum-function]]) get $T(i+m)=T(i)$: $T$ is $m$-periodic. (2) $T$ is injective on $\{0,\dots,m-1\}$, since $T(i)=T(j)$ gives $m\bigl(S_a(i)-S_a(j)\bigr)=i-j$ with $\lvert i-j\rvert<m$, forcing $i=j$. (3) For $0\le r<m$, $S_a(j+r)\le S_a(j)$ if and only if $T(j+r)\le T(j)$: with $d=S_a(j+r)-S_a(j)\in\mathbb{Z}$ one has $T(j+r)-T(j)=md-r$, which is $\le0$ when $d\le0$ (then $md-r\le-r\le0$) and is $\ge m-r\ge1$ when $d\ge1$. THE HYPOTHESIS $r<m$ IS SPENT EXACTLY HERE; say so, because it is the step a reader will skip. (4) $\{j,j+1,\dots,j+m-1\}$ is a complete set of residues modulo $m$ and $T$ is $m$-periodic, so $X(j)=\#\{i:0\le i<m,\ T(i)\le T(j)\}$: $X(j)$ is the position of $T(j)$ in the increasing order of $T(0),\dots,T(m-1)$. (5) $X$ is injective: if $T(i)<T(j)$ then $\{l:T(l)\le T(i)\}$ is a subset of $\{l:T(l)\le T(j)\}$ that omits $l=j$, so it is a proper subset of a finite set and $X(i)<X(j)$; with step 2 that makes $X$ injective. (6) $X$ lands in $\{1,\dots,m\}$, and an injection $\{0,\dots,m-1\}\to\{1,\dots,m\}$ omitting a value would be an injection of an $m$-element set into an $(m-1)$-element set, forbidden by clause 2 of [[lem-pigeonhole]]. Landmark.

items.title: The Chung–Feller theorem: for each $k$ with $0\le k\le n$, exactly $C_n$ of the diagonal paths from $(0,0)$ to $(2n,0)$ have exactly $2k$ steps lying above level $0$
items.strategy: THE SECOND CONSUMER OF THE CYCLIC-SHIFT MACHINERY, and the one it was built for. Fix the vocabulary first, in one sentence: a step of a diagonal path lies ABOVE LEVEL $0$ when both of its endpoints have height $\ge0$, and BELOW otherwise; heights differ by $1$ along a step, so exactly one of the two holds and the two counts add to $2n$. Numbered steps. (1) Let $W$ be the set of words of length $2n+1$ over $\{+1,-1\}$ with exactly $n+1$ entries $+1$, so $\lvert W\rvert=\binom{2n+1}{n}$ ([[def-binomial-coefficient]], choosing the positions of the $n$ entries $-1$). Every $a\in W$ has $\lVert a\rVert=1$, so its shift stabiliser is trivial and its orbit has exactly $2n+1$ elements ([[lem-a-word-whose-weight-is-coprime-to-its-length-has-a-trivial-shift-stabiliser]]); the orbits partition $W$ ([[thm-orbits-partition-the-set]]), so $\lvert W\rvert=(2n+1)\cdot(\text{number of orbits})$, and [[thm-catalan-numbers-by-the-cycle-lemma]] states $(2n+1)\,C_n=\binom{2n+1}{n}$, so the orbits number $C_n$ by cancelling $2n+1$ in $\mathbb{N}$. CITE THAT THEOREM FOR ITS OWN IDENTITY, never for a count of orbits, which is not its Statement. (2) BLOCKING. Fix $a\in W$ and let $t_0<\dots<t_n$ be the positions carrying $+1$, extended cyclically by $t_{l+n+1}=t_l+(2n+1)$. Put $b_l=S_a(t_{l+1})-S_a(t_l)$ for $0\le l\le n$: an integer word of length $n+1$ with $\lVert b\rVert=S_a(t_0+2n+1)-S_a(t_0)=1$, and $S_b(l)=S_a(t_l)-S_a(t_0)$. (3) Apply [[lem-shifts-of-a-weight-one-word-realise-each-count-of-nonpositive-partial-sums-once]] to $b$. Its $X(l)$ counts the $r$ with $S_a(t_{l+r})\le S_a(t_l)$, which is exactly the number of $+1$ entries of the shift $\sigma^{t_l}a$ that start at height $\le0$ measured from that shift's own start. So as $l$ runs over $0,\dots,n$ the $n+1$ shifts of $a$ that begin with $+1$ realise each of $1,\dots,n+1$ exactly once as that count. (4) Let $U\subseteq W$ be the words beginning with $+1$, so $\lvert U\rvert=\binom{2n}{n}$, which is $(n+1)C_n$ by [[cor-catalan-closed-formula]] — record the agreement. Each orbit meets $U$ in exactly $n+1$ words, one for each value $1,\dots,n+1$ by step 3, so for each such $k$ the words of $U$ with exactly $k$ initial-$+1$ positions at height $\le0$ number $C_n$, one per orbit ([[thm-sum-rule]]). (5) DELETING THE FORCED FIRST STEP. Sending $w\in U$ to the diagonal path $q$ of length $2n$ whose step word is $w_1\cdots w_{2n}$ read from $(0,0)$ is a bijection onto the diagonal paths from $(0,0)$ to $(2n,0)$, with the two-sided inverse that prepends $+1$ ([[thm-a-function-is-a-bijection-exactly-when-it-has-a-two-sided-inverse]], [[lem-lattice-paths-are-determined-by-their-step-words]]). Heights satisfy $h_w(i+1)=h_q(i)+1$, so a $+1$ entry of $w$ after the first starts at height $\le0$ exactly when the corresponding $U$ step of $q$ starts at height $\le-1$, and the deleted first entry always counts: $k=1+\#\{U\text{ steps of }q\text{ starting at height}\le-1\}$. (6) PAIRING, proved here and not assumed. For $c\in\mathbb{Z}$ the function $i\mapsto[\,h_q(i)\ge c+1\,]$ increases by $1$ exactly at a $U$ step from $c$ to $c+1$, decreases by $1$ exactly at a $D$ step from $c+1$ to $c$, and is otherwise unchanged; summing over the whole path telescopes to $[\,h_q(2n)\ge c+1\,]-[\,h_q(0)\ge c+1\,]=0$, so those two counts are equal. A step lies below level $0$ exactly when it is an up step from $c$ to $c+1$ or a down step from $c+1$ to $c$ for some $c\le-1$, so the steps of $q$ below level $0$ split evenly between $U$ and $D$ steps and number $2\bigl(k-1\bigr)$. (7) Hence $q$ has $2n-2(k-1)=2(n-k+1)$ steps above level $0$, and as $k$ runs over $1,\dots,n+1$ the value $n-k+1$ runs over $n,\dots,0$. Conclude the statement in the title. Check $n=1$ by hand against $UD$ and $DU$, and $n=2$ against the six paths, where each of $k=0,1,2$ has two. Landmark.

items.title: Every Dyck path of semilength $n+1$ factors uniquely as $U\,P\,D\,Q$ with $P\in\mathcal{D}_i$ and $Q\in\mathcal{D}_{n-i}$
items.strategy: Let $w$ be a Dyck path of semilength $n+1$. Its first step is $U$; let $2i+2$ be the least positive index at which the height returns to $0$ (it exists because $h(2n+2)=0$). Then $w=U\,P\,D\,Q$ where $P$ is the step word strictly between positions $1$ and $2i+1$ and $Q$ the remainder. Prove $P\in\mathcal{D}_i$ (heights inside are $\ge1$, so shifting down by one keeps them $\ge0$) and $Q\in\mathcal{D}_{n-i}$, and prove uniqueness by showing $i$ is determined as the first return. Then exhibit the inverse map $(i,P,Q)\mapsto UPDQ$ and check it lands in $\mathcal{D}_{n+1}$. The result is a bijection $\mathcal{D}_{n+1}\to\coprod_{i=0}^{n}\mathcal{D}_i\times\mathcal{D}_{n-i}$. Landmark: three later theorems on this page are this lemma applied to a different family.

items.title: $C_{n+1}=\sum_{i=0}^{n}C_i\,C_{n-i}$, with $C_0=1$
items.strategy: Count the disjoint union of [[lem-first-return-decomposition-of-a-nonempty-dyck-path]] with [[thm-sum-rule]] and [[thm-product-rule]]; the index set is $\{0,\dots,n\}$ and the sum is the natural-number sum of [[def-sum-over-a-finite-index-set]]. Check $n=0$ ($C_1=C_0C_0=1$) and $n=1$ ($C_2=2$). Landmark.

items.title: The Catalan generating function $C(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}C_nx^n$ in $\mathbb{Q}\llbracket x\rrbracket$
items.strategy: Define $C\in\mathbb{Q}\llbracket x\rrbracket$ as the formal power series ([[def-formal-power-series-and-coefficient-extraction]]) whose coefficient at $n$ is the rational number determined by the natural number $C_n$. Say once, in a Remark, that a count is being read as a rational coefficient and that the identification is the ring embedding of $\mathbb{N}$ into $\mathbb{Q}$; do not write the canonical embedding applied to $C_n$ anywhere. Work in $\mathbb{Q}\llbracket x\rrbracket$ rather than $\mathbb{Z}\llbracket x\rrbracket$ because the square-root and binomial machinery this page cites needs a $\mathbb{Q}$-algebra.

items.title: $C(x)=1+x\,C(x)^2$
items.strategy: Compare coefficients: $[x^{n+1}]\bigl(xC^2\bigr)=[x^{n}]C^2=\sum_{i=0}^{n}C_iC_{n-i}$ by the Cauchy product of [[prop-coefficient-extraction-linearity-and-extensionality]], which is $C_{n+1}$ by [[thm-catalan-recurrence]]; and the constant coefficients agree because $C_0=1$. Conclude by extensionality. Landmark.

items.title: $[x^k](1-4x)^{1/2}=-\frac{2}{k}\binom{2k-2}{k-1}$ for $k\ge1$, and $1$ for $k=0$
items.strategy: Expand $(1+u)^{1/2}$ with $u=-4x$ by the formal binomial power law of [[thm-formal-exponential-logarithm-identities]], giving $[x^k]=\binom{1/2}{k}(-4)^k$ where $\binom{1/2}{k}$ is the displayed falling-factorial quotient. Then prove the closed form $\binom{1/2}{k}(-4)^k=-\frac{2}{k}\binom{2k-2}{k-1}$ for $k\ge1$ by induction on $k$, checking the ratio of consecutive terms; state the $k=1$ base ($-2$) explicitly. Cross-check the first coefficients against $1-2x-2x^2-4x^3-10x^4-28x^5$. THE INDEX $k=0$ IS SEPARATE and the formula in the title is false there, which is why it is stated with the range.

items.title: $2x\,C(x)=1-(1-4x)^{1/2}$, where $(1-4x)^{1/2}$ is the unique square root with constant coefficient $1$
items.strategy: From $C=1+xC^2$ get $(1-2xC)^2=1-4x$ by expanding; the series $1-2xC$ lies in $1+x\mathbb{Q}\llbracket x\rrbracket$, so by the UNIQUENESS clause of [[cor-unique-formal-root-with-constant-one]] it IS $(1-4x)^{1/2}$. This is the whole point of the item: the root is identified, never chosen. Do not divide by $2x$, which is not a unit; state the identity in the cleared form of the title and derive coefficient statements from it. Landmark.

items.title: A third derivation of $(n+1)\,C_n=\binom{2n}{n}$, from the closed form of $C(x)$
items.strategy: Take $[x^{n+1}]$ of both sides of [[thm-catalan-generating-function-closed-form]]: the left is $2C_n$ and the right is $-[x^{n+1}](1-4x)^{1/2}=\frac{2}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}$ by [[lem-the-coefficients-of-the-formal-square-root-of-one-minus-four-x]]. Clear the denominator to reach the $\mathbb{N}$ identity and record explicitly that this proof and [[thm-catalan-numbers-by-reflection]] and [[thm-catalan-numbers-by-the-cycle-lemma]] agree. The route is genuinely different: no bijection and no group action, only formal algebra in $\mathbb{Q}\llbracket x\rrbracket$.

items.title: $C(x)$ is not a rational formal power series, so $(C_n)$ satisfies no eventual constant-coefficient linear recurrence
items.strategy:
Suppose $QC=P$ with $P,Q\in\mathbb{Q}[x]$ and $Q(0)
e0$, in the sense of [[def-rational-formal-power-series-and-reduced-denominator]]. Put $R=Q-2xP$, a polynomial; from $(1-2xC)^2=1-4x$ multiply through by $Q^2$ to get $R^2=(1-4x)Q^2$ in $\mathbb{Q}[x]$. Then $R
e0$ (else $1-4x=0$) and $Q
e0$, so comparing degrees gives $2\deg R=1+2\deg Q$, impossible by parity. The recurrence clause is then [[thm-linear-recurrence-iff-rational-generating-function]] read in the contrapositive. THE SEAM WITH THE PRECEDING PAGE, and the item that makes the companion page's false statement refutable in three steps.

items.title: Motzkin paths, Schröder paths, the Motzkin numbers $M_n$, the large Schröder numbers $R_n$, and their generating functions
items.strategy: Two more instances of [[def-lattice-path-and-step-set]], and nothing new is needed to state them. A **Motzkin path of length $n$** is a lattice path with steps in $\{U,D,L\}$, where $U=(1,1)$, $D=(1,-1)$ and $L=(1,0)$, from $(0,0)$ to $(n,0)$ whose vertices all have second coordinate $\ge0$. A **Schröder path of half-length $n$** is a lattice path with steps in $\{U,D,L_2\}$, where $L_2=(2,0)$, from $(0,0)$ to $(2n,0)$ whose vertices all have second coordinate $\ge0$. Write $\mathcal{M}_n$ and $\mathcal{R}_n$ for the two sets. WELL-DEFINEDNESS, the same obligation [[def-catalan-number]] discharges: each set injects into the words over its three-element step set by [[lem-lattice-paths-are-determined-by-their-step-words]], and those words have bounded length — exactly $n$ for a Motzkin path of length $n$, and AT MOST $2n$ for a Schröder path of half-length $n$, whose step count $n+k$ depends on its number $k$ of up steps and so is NOT determined by $n$, and a subset of a finite set is finite ([[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]]), so both are finite; list those two in `justified_by`, not in `deps`. DEFINE $M_n:=\lvert\mathcal{M}_n\rvert$, the **Motzkin numbers**, and $R_n:=\lvert\mathcal{R}_n\rvert$, the **large Schröder numbers**, AS COUNTS and never by a formula, and record $M_0=1$, $M_1=1$, $M_2=2$ and $R_0=1$, $R_1=2$ directly from the definition: at $n=0$ the empty path is the only one, which is where $M_0=R_0=1$ comes from. Then define $M(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}M_nx^n$ and $R(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}R_nx^n$ in $\mathbb{Q}\llbracket x\rrbracket$ ([[def-formal-power-series-and-coefficient-extraction]]), reading each count as a rational coefficient exactly as [[def-catalan-generating-function]] does. TWO CONVENTIONS TO FIX EXPLICITLY, because both are places a reader is misled. First, $x$ marks LENGTH in $M(x)$ but HALF-LENGTH in $R(x)$; that is the indexing of the source, and it is what makes the two functional equations below differ. Second, the source writes $S_n$ for the large Schröder numbers and this page writes $R_n$, because $S$ is already the step set of [[def-lattice-path-and-step-set]] and $S_a$ the partial-sum function of [[def-cyclic-shift-and-the-periodic-partial-sum-function]]. Record the step count that both proofs below use: a Schröder path of half-length $n$ with $k$ up steps has $k$ down steps and $n-k$ level steps, hence $n+k$ steps in all. Landmark.

items.title: $M(x)=1+x\,M(x)+x^{2}M(x)^{2}$, and $2x^{2}M(x)=1-x-(1-2x-3x^{2})^{1/2}$
items.strategy: The page's own route, run a second time on a third step set; no symbolic method and no fixed-point theorem is used anywhere. Numbered steps. (1) FIRST RETURN. A Motzkin path of length $n+1$ is nonempty, so its first step is $L$ or $U$. If $L$, deleting it leaves a Motzkin path of length $n$. If $U$, let $j$ be the least positive index with height $0$ — it exists because the path ends at height $0$ — so the step arriving at $j$ is $D$, and the path is $U\,P\,D\,Q$ with $P$ the piece strictly between, lowered by one, a Motzkin path of length $i$, and $Q$ a Motzkin path of length $n-1-i$. Uniqueness holds because $i$ is determined as the first return; give the inverse $(i,P,Q)\mapsto UPDQ$ explicitly ([[thm-a-function-is-a-bijection-exactly-when-it-has-a-two-sided-inverse]]). This is [[lem-first-return-decomposition-of-a-nonempty-dyck-path]] with a level step added, and the added case is the whole difference. (2) COUNT: $M_{n+1}=M_n+\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}M_iM_{n-1-i}$ by [[thm-sum-rule]] and [[thm-product-rule]] over the index set $\{0,\dots,n-1\}$ of [[def-sum-over-a-finite-index-set]]. THE SUM IS EMPTY AT $n=0$, giving $M_1=M_0=1$, which is correct because no path of length $1$ that begins with $U$ can return to height $0$; check that case explicitly. (3) COMPARE COEFFICIENTS: $[x^{n+1}]\bigl(xM+x^2M^2\bigr)=M_n+\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}M_iM_{n-1-i}$ by the Cauchy product of [[prop-coefficient-extraction-linearity-and-extensionality]], the constant coefficients agree because $M_0=1$, and extensionality gives the functional equation. (4) COMPLETE THE SQUARE. From $x^2M^2+(x-1)M+1=0$, multiply by $4x^2$: $\bigl(2x^2M+x-1\bigr)^2=(x-1)^2-4x^2=1-2x-3x^2$. (5) IDENTIFY THE ROOT, never choose it. $1-x-2x^2M$ has constant coefficient $1$, and $1-2x-3x^2=1+u$ with $u=-2x-3x^2\in x\mathbb{Q}\llbracket x\rrbracket$, so the UNIQUENESS clause of [[cor-unique-formal-root-with-constant-one]] says $1-x-2x^2M$ IS $(1-2x-3x^2)^{1/2}$. Do not divide by $2x^2$, which is not a unit; state the identity in the cleared form of the title, exactly as [[thm-catalan-generating-function-closed-form]] does. (6) Check the first coefficients against $M_0,\dots,M_4=1,1,2,4,9$. Landmark.

items.title: $M_n=\sum_{k\in\mathbb{N},\,2k\le n}\binom{n}{2k}C_k$
items.strategy: DELETE THE LEVEL STEPS: a bijective proof, so it is a genuinely different route from the generating function of [[thm-motzkin-numbers-by-first-return-decomposition]], and it is the identity that makes the Catalan numbers of this page count something else. A Motzkin path of length $n$ is determined by the set $A\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\}$ of positions carrying a non-level step together with the word those positions carry, by [[lem-lattice-paths-are-determined-by-their-step-words]]. A level step changes no height, so the height condition on the whole path is exactly the height condition on that subword; the subword therefore has equally many $U$ and $D$ letters and every prefix at least as many $U$ as $D$, which is to say it is the step word of a Dyck path of semilength $k$ where $\lvert A\rvert=2k$ ([[def-dyck-path-and-semilength]]). The map to $\bigl(k,A,\text{Dyck path}\bigr)$ has the obvious two-sided inverse ([[thm-a-function-is-a-bijection-exactly-when-it-has-a-two-sided-inverse]]). Count with [[thm-sum-rule]] and [[thm-product-rule]] over the finite index set $\{k\in\mathbb{N}:2k\le n\}$, using $\#\{A\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\}:\lvert A\rvert=2k\}=\binom{n}{2k}$, which is what [[def-binomial-coefficient]] defines a binomial coefficient to be. STATE WHY $\lvert A\rvert$ IS EVEN rather than assuming it. Check $n=0,\dots,4$ against $1,1,2,4,9$; at $n=0$ the index set is $\{0\}$ and the single term is $\binom{0}{0}C_0=1$.

items.title: $R(x)=1+x\,R(x)+x\,R(x)^{2}$, and $2x\,R(x)=1-x-(1-6x+x^{2})^{1/2}$
items.strategy: The same six steps as [[thm-motzkin-numbers-by-first-return-decomposition]] with the level step widened to $L_2=(2,0)$, and ONE INDEX RANGE THAT GENUINELY DIFFERS; the difference is the whole content of this item and must be a numbered step, not a remark. (1) FIRST RETURN. A Schröder path of half-length $n+1$ begins with $L_2$ or with $U$. If $L_2$, deleting it leaves a Schröder path of half-length $n$. If $U$, the first return to height $0$ arrives by a $D$ and the path is $U\,P\,D\,Q$ with $P$ a Schröder path of half-length $i$ lowered by one and $Q$ a Schröder path of half-length $n-i$: the $U$ and the $D$ together consume two units of horizontal extent, hence exactly ONE unit of half-length, so the convolution index runs $i=0,\dots,n$ and NOT $i=0,\dots,n-1$ as in the Motzkin case. Give the inverse explicitly. (2) COUNT: $R_{n+1}=R_n+\sum_{i=0}^{n}R_iR_{n-i}$ by [[thm-sum-rule]] and [[thm-product-rule]]. At $n=0$ the sum has the single term $R_0R_0=1$, giving $R_1=2$, and the two paths are $L_2$ and $UD$; check that. (3) COMPARE COEFFICIENTS to get $R=1+xR+xR^2$, the constant coefficients agreeing because $R_0=1$. (4) COMPLETE THE SQUARE. From $xR^2+(x-1)R+1=0$, multiply by $4x$: $\bigl(2xR+x-1\bigr)^2=(x-1)^2-4x=1-6x+x^2$. (5) IDENTIFY THE ROOT: $1-x-2xR$ has constant coefficient $1$ and $1-6x+x^2=1+u$ with $u=-6x+x^2\in x\mathbb{Q}\llbracket x\rrbracket$, so the uniqueness clause of [[cor-unique-formal-root-with-constant-one]] identifies it as $(1-6x+x^2)^{1/2}$. Do not divide by $2x$. (6) Check against $R_0,\dots,R_4=1,2,6,22,90$. Landmark.

items.title: $R_n=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n+k}{2k}C_k$
items.strategy: The level-step deletion of [[cor-motzkin-numbers-as-a-binomial-sum-of-catalan-numbers]] again, with the step count that [[def-motzkin-and-schroder-paths]] records doing the work: a Schröder path of half-length $n$ with $k$ up steps has $n-k$ level steps and therefore $n+k$ steps in all, so the positions available to the non-level steps number $n+k$ and depend on $k$ — that dependence is why the binomial coefficient is $\binom{n+k}{2k}$ and not $\binom{n}{2k}$, and it is the one thing to state plainly. The path is determined by which $2k$ of those $n+k$ positions carry non-level steps together with the word they carry, which is the step word of a Dyck path of semilength $k$ for the same reason as in the Motzkin corollary. Count with [[thm-sum-rule]] and [[thm-product-rule]] over $\{0,\dots,n\}$, using [[def-binomial-coefficient]] as a count of subsets. Check $n=0,\dots,3$ against $1,2,6,22$; at $n=1$ the two terms are $\binom{1}{0}C_0=1$ and $\binom{2}{2}C_1=1$.

items.title: Balanced bracket words, defined by the recursive grammar
items.strategy: Define $\mathcal{B}\subseteq\{\texttt{(},\texttt{)}\}^{*}$ RECURSIVELY, not by a counting condition: $\mathcal{B}_0=\{\varepsilon\}$ and, for $n\ge0$, $\mathcal{B}_{n+1}$ is the set of words $\texttt{(}\,u\,\texttt{)}\,v$ with $u\in\mathcal{B}_i$, $v\in\mathcal{B}_{n-i}$ for some $0\le i\le n$. Justify the recursion by strong induction on the length. THE RECURSIVE DEFINITION IS THE POINT: taking the prefix condition as the definition would make the next theorem vacuous. Record that $\mathcal{B}_n$ is a set of words of length $2n$ and is finite.

items.title: $\mathcal{B}_n$ is exactly the set of words of length $2n$ over $\{\texttt{(},\texttt{)}\}$ in which every prefix has at least as many $\texttt{(}$ as $\texttt{)}$ and the totals are equal
items.strategy: Two inclusions, each by induction. Forward: a word built by the grammar satisfies the prefix condition, by induction on $n$ and the concatenation behaviour of prefix counts. Backward: given a word $w$ satisfying the prefix condition, transport it to a Dyck path by $\texttt{(}\mapsto U$, $\texttt{)}\mapsto D$ and apply [[lem-first-return-decomposition-of-a-nonempty-dyck-path]] to obtain the grammar factorisation; induct on $n$. The transport is a bijection of alphabets and must be stated as such. Landmark.

items.title: $\lvert\mathcal{B}_n\rvert=C_n$
items.strategy: The alphabet bijection of [[thm-balanced-bracket-words-are-exactly-the-nonnegative-prefix-words]] carries $\mathcal{B}_n$ onto the set of ballot words of length $2n$, which is $\mathcal{D}_n$ under step words. Transport of cardinality along a bijection is [[def-finite-cardinality]].

items.title: Binary trees, defined recursively, and their size
items.strategy: Define the set $\mathcal{T}$ of **binary trees** by recursion on size: $\mathcal{T}_0=\{\bullet\}$ where $\bullet$ is a fixed object (the empty tree), and $\mathcal{T}_{n+1}=\coprod_{i=0}^{n}\mathcal{T}_i\times\mathcal{T}_{n-i}$, so that a tree of size $n+1$ is an ordered pair $(L,R)$ of trees whose sizes add to $n$; the **size** is the number of internal nodes. Make the recursion legitimate by defining $\mathcal{T}_n$ by strong recursion on $n$ and proving the union is disjoint. NO GRAPH THEORY IS USED OR AVAILABLE: a binary tree here is an element of an inductively defined set of ordered pairs, and the Remark says so. Landmark.

items.title: Each $\mathcal{T}_n$ is finite
items.strategy: Strong induction on $n$ using [[thm-sum-rule]] and [[thm-product-rule]] on the defining disjoint union. This is the well-definedness obligation that lets $\lvert\mathcal{T}_n\rvert$ be spoken of at all.

items.title: There is a bijection $\mathcal{T}_n\to\mathcal{D}_n$ for every $n$
items.strategy: Define $\Phi_n:\mathcal{T}_n\to\mathcal{D}_n$ by recursion: $\Phi_0(\bullet)$ is the empty path, and $\Phi_{n+1}(L,R)=U\,\Phi_i(L)\,D\,\Phi_{n-i}(R)$ where $i$ is the size of $L$. Prove it is a bijection by strong induction, using [[lem-first-return-decomposition-of-a-nonempty-dyck-path]] to build the inverse: the first-return factorisation of a Dyck path is exactly the pair $(L,R)$. BIJECTIVITY IS PROVED FROM THE FIRST-RETURN LEMMA, not drawn. Landmark.

items.title: $\lvert\mathcal{T}_n\rvert=C_n$
items.strategy: Transport of cardinality along the bijection of [[thm-binary-trees-correspond-to-dyck-paths]].

items.title: Chords of a labelled convex polygon, crossing, and triangulations, defined combinatorially
items.strategy: For $m\ge3$ let the vertices be $1<2<\cdots<m$ in cyclic order. A **chord** is a pair $\{i,j\}$ with $i<j$; it is a **side** when $j=i+1$ or $(i,j)=(1,m)$, and a **diagonal** otherwise. Two chords $\{i,j\}$ and $\{k,l\}$ **cross** when $i<k<j<l$ or $k<i<l<j$. A **triangulation of the $m$-gon** is a set of pairwise non-crossing diagonals that is maximal with that property; write $\mathcal{P}_m$ for the set of triangulations. NO GEOMETRY, NO PLANE, NO AREA: the definition is a condition on integers, which is the only form available at this order, and the Remark says the geometric picture is an illustration, not a hypothesis. Record $\mathcal{P}_3=\{\varnothing\}$. Landmark.

items.title: For $m\ge3$ and a triangulation $T$ of the $m$-gon there is a unique $k$ with $1<k<m$ such that $\{1,k\}$ and $\{k,m\}$ are both chords of $T$ or sides, and $T$ splits along $k$
items.strategy: Take $k$ least in $\{2,\dots,m-1\}$ such that $\{k,m\}$ lies in $T$ or is the side $\{m-1,m\}$; such $k$ exists since $k=m-1$ qualifies. Show $\{1,k\}$ is a side or lies in $T$: otherwise it is a diagonal not in $T$, so maximality gives some $\{p,q\}\in T$ crossing it, that is $1<p<k<q$; if $q<m$ then $\{p,q\}$ crosses $\{k,m\}$, and if $q=m$ then $p<k$ contradicts minimality. Next show every chord of $T$ has both endpoints in $\{1,\dots,k\}$ or both in $\{k,\dots,m\}$, again by crossing with $\{k,m\}$ or minimality. Finally show the two restrictions are triangulations of the sub-polygons and that the construction is reversible, so $\mathcal{P}_m\to\coprod_{k=2}^{m-1}\mathcal{P}_{k}\times\mathcal{P}_{m-k+1}$ is a bijection (a sub-polygon on the vertices $1,\dots,k$ has $k$ vertices, and one on $k,\dots,m$ has $m-k+1$). Uniqueness of $k$ is part of the claim and needs its own step.

items.title: There is a bijection $\mathcal{T}_n\to\mathcal{P}_{n+2}$ for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$
items.strategy: Recursion on $n$ using [[lem-a-triangulation-has-a-unique-triangle-on-the-closing-side]] against the defining recursion of [[def-binary-tree-and-its-size]]: both are the same disjoint union over a split point, so the two recursions match term by term. Handle $n=0$ ($\mathcal{T}_0$ and $\mathcal{P}_2$ — state the convention that the $2$-gon has the single empty triangulation, or start at $n=1$ with $\mathcal{P}_3$ and treat $n=0$ separately; FIX THIS BOUNDARY EXPLICITLY, it is where an off-by-one lives). Landmark.

items.title: $\lvert\mathcal{P}_{n+2}\rvert=C_n$
items.strategy: Compose the bijections of [[thm-triangulations-of-a-convex-polygon-correspond-to-binary-trees]] and [[thm-binary-trees-correspond-to-dyck-paths]] and transport cardinality. Record $\lvert\mathcal{P}_6\rvert=C_4=14$ as the instance the companion page exhibits.

items.title: Path systems between two families of lattice points, and non-intersecting systems
items.strategy: Fix $A_1,\dots,A_r$ and $E_1,\dots,E_r$ in $\mathbb{Z}^2$. For $\pi\in S_r$ ([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]]) a **$\pi$-system** is an $r$-tuple $(P_1,\dots,P_r)$ with $P_i$ a monotone lattice path from $A_i$ to $E_{\pi(i)}$. Two paths **intersect** when they share a lattice point, that is when the images of their point functions meet. A system is **non-intersecting** when no two of its paths intersect. Record that the set of $\pi$-systems is finite, by [[thm-monotone-lattice-paths-in-a-rectangle-are-counted-by-a-binomial-coefficient]] and [[thm-product-rule]].

items.title: Tail-swapping is a sign-reversing involution on the intersecting systems
items.strategy: On the set of pairs $(\pi,\text{system})$ with the system intersecting, define $\iota$ as follows: take the least $i$ such that $P_i$ meets some later path, then the least $j>i$ with $P_i\cap P_j\ne\varnothing$, then the first point of $P_i$ (in path order) lying on $P_j$; swap the tails of $P_i$ and $P_j$ at that point. Prove: the result is again a system, for the permutation $\pi\circ(i\ j)$; the choices $(i,j,\text{point})$ are unchanged by the swap, so $\iota\circ\iota$ is the identity; and $\operatorname{sgn}(\pi\circ(i\,j))=-\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)$ by [[thm-sign-is-a-homomorphism]]. EVERY CHOICE MUST BE CANONICAL, or the involution is not well defined; that is the only difficulty in the argument and each choice gets its own numbered step. Landmark.

items.title: $\det\bigl(\lvert\mathcal{M}(A_i,E_j)\rvert\bigr)_{i,j}=\sum_{\pi\in S_r}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)\cdot\#\{\text{non-intersecting }\pi\text{-systems}\}$
items.strategy: Expand the determinant by its Leibniz definition ([[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]) over $\mathbb{Z}$: the term at $\pi$ is $\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)$ times the number of $\pi$-systems, by [[thm-product-rule]]. Split each term into intersecting and non-intersecting systems; the intersecting parts cancel in pairs under [[lem-sign-reversing-involution-on-intersecting-path-systems]], leaving the stated sum. State the theorem as an identity in $\mathbb{Z}$. Add the standard clause: when the configuration is **compatible**, meaning every path $A_i\to E_j$ meets every path $A_k\to E_l$ whenever $i<k$ and $j>l$, only $\pi=\mathrm{id}$ contributes and the determinant is the number of non-intersecting systems joining $A_i$ to $E_i$. This is the lattice-path case of Krattenthaler Theorem 10.13.1; say so rather than claiming the general acyclic-digraph statement, which needs digraph machinery this page does not build. Landmark.

items.title: For $n\ge1$ the pairs of non-intersecting monotone paths $(1,0)\to(n+1,n)$ and $(0,1)\to(n,n+1)$ number $\binom{2n}{n}^2-\binom{2n}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n-1}$
items.strategy: Apply [[thm-lindstrom-gessel-viennot]] with $A_1=(1,0)$, $A_2=(0,1)$, $E_1=(n+1,n)$, $E_2=(n,n+1)$; the four entries are $\binom{2n}{n}$, $\binom{2n}{n+1}$, $\binom{2n}{n-1}$, $\binom{2n}{n}$ by the rectangle count. Compatibility must be PROVED, not assumed: show every monotone path $A_1\to E_2$ meets every monotone path $A_2\to E_1$, by tracking the sign of $y-x$ along each path and applying the same discrete change-of-side argument as [[lem-a-diagonal-path-that-changes-side-of-a-level-meets-it]] through the dictionary [[lem-monotone-and-diagonal-lattice-paths-correspond]]. Check $n=1$ by hand: the determinant is $2^2-1\cdot1=3$, and the four pairs minus the one pair meeting at $(1,1)$ is $3$.

items.title: Why the Catalan count is proved three times, and how the three statements agree
items.strategy: Say what each route uses and what it does not: the reflection route is a bijection between two sets of paths; the cycle-lemma route is a free action of $\mathbb{Z}/(2n+1)$; the generating-function route is formal algebra in $\mathbb{Q}\llbracket x\rrbracket$ resting on the uniqueness of a constant-one square root. Record the two arithmetic identities that make the three conclusions the same statement, each pointing at the numbered step that proves it. A JUSTIFYING REMARK, not a survey: it says why the hypotheses of each route differ, and it names no page other than this one. Do not count anything.

items.title: The trees and polygons of this page are defined by recursion and by inequalities on labels
items.strategy: State plainly that [[def-binary-tree-and-its-size]] is an inductively defined set of ordered pairs and carries no vertex set, edge set or connectivity, and that [[def-convex-polygon-chords-crossings-and-triangulations]] is a condition on integers with no plane, no segment and no area. Say which properties are therefore NOT available here: nothing about drawings, and nothing from the graph-theoretic notion of a tree, which is not among this page's declared prerequisites. Declare the graph-theoretic tree items in \`forward_refs\` for orientation only and check with \`fwdcheck\` that the target page is strictly later in plan order. Do not write that the library "does not develop" anything.

items.title: Conventions fixed on this page
items.strategy: One paragraph per convention, each pointing at the item that fixes it: the two step sets and the dictionary between them; $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, so every index range is checked at its first index and $C_0=1$; semilength versus length; "strictly above" versus "weakly above" a level; the cycle lemma's orientation (strict positivity of every partial sum, shifts indexed by their starting position), where the sources genuinely disagree; and that a bijection on this page is always given with a two-sided inverse. Close with the results this page states but does not build, naming for each what it would need and never with a bare "not built here". The **Hankel determinant** $\det(C_{i+j})_{0\le i,j\le n-1}=1$ would need [[thm-lindstrom-gessel-viennot]] restated for a family of monotone paths closed under tail-swapping at a common point — the paths weakly below a fixed diagonal are such a family, and the tail-swap of [[lem-sign-reversing-involution-on-intersecting-path-systems]] stays inside it — together with the count of the monotone paths from $(0,0)$ to $(m,m)$ that stay weakly below the diagonal, which this page does not state as a result of its own; the theorem needs both, and this page supplies neither. The **Narayana refinement** of $C_n$ by the number of peaks counts Dyck paths by a statistic on them, and no route to $C_n$ built here — reflection, the cycle lemma, the generating function — tracks the number of peaks; the refinement needs machinery this page does not build. It is not a missing source: Huq §2.5 carries the formulas and lies outside this page’s declared read range. Say "not built here", never "the library does not develop".

title: Lattice Paths and Catalan Numbers — Examples

items.title: The ten monotone lattice paths from $(0,0)$ to $(3,2)$
items.strategy: List all ten step words in $\{E,N\}^5$ with two $N$s, alongside the two-element subset of $\{0,1,2,3,4\}$ each corresponds to, and check $\binom{5}{2}=10$. Verify the boundary claims of the theorem too: one path to $(3,0)$ and one to $(0,0)$.

items.title: The five Dyck paths of semilength $3$, with their height functions
items.strategy: Write out $UUUDDD$, $UUDUDD$, $UUDDUD$, $UDUUDD$, $UDUDUD$ with the height sequence of each, and check each stays $\ge0$. Then verify $C_3=5$ against $(3+1)C_3=\binom{6}{3}=20$. A \`tikz\` figure of the five paths is welcome in the Example section, with every fact used also written in the text.

items.title: The five Dyck paths of semilength $3$ matched to bracket words, binary trees and pentagon triangulations
items.strategy: Tabulate the five objects of each family and the images under $\Phi_3$ of [[thm-binary-trees-correspond-to-dyck-paths]] and under the triangulation bijection, so a reader sees the correspondences as functions and not as a coincidence of counts. Give the bracket words explicitly and the triangulations as their diagonal sets, e.g. $\{\{1,3\},\{1,4\}\}$ on the pentagon.

items.title: Reflecting a path from $(0,0)$ to $(6,0)$ at its first visit to level $-1$
items.strategy: Take $UDDUDU$ (heights $0,1,0,-1,0,-1,0$), find the first visit to $-1$ at index $3$, reflect the initial segment, and check the image is a path from $(0,-2)$ to $(6,0)$. Apply the reflection twice and check the original returns. Then count: $\binom{6}{3}=20$ paths in total, $\binom{6}{4}=15$ touching $-1$, and $C_3=5$.

items.title: The ballot problem for $p=3$, $q=2$: two orderings out of ten
items.strategy: List the ten orderings of three $A$ votes and two $B$ votes, mark the two in which $A$ leads after every vote ($AAABB$ and $AABAB$), and check $(p+q)N=(p-q)\binom{p+q}{p}$, i.e. $5\cdot 2=1\cdot 10$. Then check the weak count for $p=q=2$ against $C_2=2$.

items.title: The seven cyclic shifts of a $\pm1$ word of weight $1$, exactly one with all partial sums positive
items.strategy: Take $a=(-1,+1,+1,-1,+1,-1,+1)$ of length $7$ with three $-1$s, weight $1$. Tabulate all seven shifts with their partial-sum sequences, mark the unique good one, and delete its leading $+1$ to obtain a Dyck path of semilength $3$. Then check the count $(2\cdot3+1)C_3=\binom{7}{3}$, i.e. $7\cdot5=35$. Also exhibit a word with weight $2$ where exactly two shifts are good, so the general statement is seen and not only the case used.

items.title: $C_0$ to $C_6$ by the recurrence and by the closed formula
items.strategy: Compute $1,1,2,5,14,42,132$ from [[thm-catalan-recurrence]], then again from $(n+1)C_n=\binom{2n}{n}$, tabulating $\binom{2n}{n}=1,2,6,20,70,252,924$. Do not describe the table; give it.

items.title: The fourteen triangulations of the convex hexagon
items.strategy: Enumerate all fourteen maximal non-crossing diagonal sets on vertices $1,\dots,6$, grouped by the value of $k$ supplied by [[lem-a-triangulation-has-a-unique-triangle-on-the-closing-side]], and check the total against $C_4=14$ and against $\sum_{k=2}^{5}\lvert\mathcal{P}_k\rvert\lvert\mathcal{P}_{7-k}\rvert$. Each triangulation is a set of three diagonals; write them out.

items.title: Squaring the truncation of $C(x)$ and of $(1-4x)^{1/2}$ through degree five
items.strategy: Check $C=1+xC^2$ coefficientwise through $x^5$ using $1,1,2,5,14,42$, and check $(1-2xC)^2\equiv1-4x$ modulo $x^6$ using the coefficients $1,-2,-2,-4,-10,-28$ supplied by [[lem-the-coefficients-of-the-formal-square-root-of-one-minus-four-x]]. Every product coefficient is a finite Cauchy convolution; display them.

items.title: The three non-intersecting path pairs at $n=1$, counted by hand and by the determinant
items.strategy: List the two paths $(1,0)\to(2,1)$ and the two paths $(0,1)\to(1,2)$, list the four pairs, identify the single pair meeting at $(1,1)$, and check $3=\binom{2}{1}^2-\binom{2}{2}\binom{2}{0}$. Then do $n=2$ if it stays short, checking $\binom42^2-\binom43\binom41=36-16=20$ against a direct count.

items.title: Tail-swapping applied to an intersecting pair, and applied twice
items.strategy: Take a concrete intersecting pair of monotone paths, identify the canonical intersection point selected by [[lem-sign-reversing-involution-on-intersecting-path-systems]], swap the tails, note that the permutation changes from the identity to the transposition, and apply the map again to recover the original. This is the item that shows why the choices have to be canonical.

items.title: FALSE: $\binom{2n}{n}/(n+1)$ is a natural number only for small $n$
items.strategy: State the false claim in the form a reader might believe — that the divisibility is an accident of small cases. Refute in two steps from [[cor-one-more-than-n-divides-the-central-binomial-coefficient]]: the quotient is the count $C_n$ for EVERY $n$, so it is a natural number for every $n$. Add a table for $n\le6$ so the refutation is also visible. The Refutation must not merely assert the corollary; it must say why a divisibility proved by exhibiting a count needs no arithmetic.

items.title: FALSE: the monotone paths from $(0,0)$ to $(n,n)$ that stay weakly below the diagonal number $\binom{2n}{n}/2$
items.strategy: The plausible symmetry argument is that "below" and "above" split the paths evenly; it fails because paths touching the diagonal lie in both classes. Refute at $n=2$: there are $\binom42=6$ paths, the weakly-below ones number $C_2=2$, and $6/2=3$. Then give the general reason, citing [[lem-monotone-and-diagonal-lattice-paths-correspond]] to convert "weakly below the diagonal" into "height $\le0$" and [[cor-catalan-closed-formula]] for the true value $C_n$. Name the exact step of the false argument that breaks.

items.title: FALSE: the Catalan numbers satisfy a constant-coefficient linear recurrence
items.strategy: The claim is tempting because $C_{n+1}=\sum_iC_iC_{n-i}$ IS a recurrence — but not a linear one with constant coefficients. Refute by [[thm-the-catalan-generating-function-is-not-rational]] together with [[thm-linear-recurrence-iff-rational-generating-function]]. Say in the Refutation exactly which hypothesis of the recurrence–rationality theorem the convolution recurrence fails.

items.title: A natural-looking map from hexagon triangulations to Dyck paths that is not injective
items.strategy: Define $f$ on $\mathcal{P}_6$ by sending a triangulation to the weakly decreasing list of the "fan sizes" at its vertices, or another visibly natural statistic, and EXHIBIT TWO DISTINCT TRIANGULATIONS WITH THE SAME VALUE, written out as diagonal sets. The point of the item is that equal cardinality plus a natural-looking rule is not a bijection: bijectivity on this page is always proved by a two-sided inverse. Choose the statistic so the collision is checkable in two lines, and verify the collision explicitly before shipping.

items.title: With steps $(1,1)$ and $(1,-2)$ a path can pass from above a level to below it without meeting it
items.strategy: Take the step set $\{(1,1),(1,-2)\}$ and the one-step path from $(0,1)$ to $(1,-1)$: it starts above level $0$ and ends below it and never has height $0$, so [[lem-a-diagonal-path-that-changes-side-of-a-level-meets-it]] fails and the reflection map of [[lem-reflection-at-the-first-visit-to-a-level-is-a-bijection]] is undefined. Then show the count itself fails: exhibit a small pair of endpoints for this step set where "total minus reflected" gives the wrong number, computed by listing paths. THE ITEM IS ABOUT THE HYPOTHESIS, so the Refutation names the exact step of the reflection lemma that uses $\lvert h(i)-h(i-1)\rvert=1$.

items.title: The incidence vector $v_A\in F^{n}$ of a subset $A\subseteq[n]$ over a stated field
items.strategy: For a field $F$, $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $A\subseteq[n]=\{0,\dots,n-1\}$, define $v_A\in F^{n}$ by $(v_A)_i=1_F$ when $i\in A$ and $0_F$ otherwise. Prove the two facts every later item uses: $A\mapsto v_A$ is injective for every field (compare coordinates), and $v_\varnothing=0$. THE FIELD IS PART OF THE DATA and is written into the notation whenever two fields are in play on the same page; the whole page turns on which field is chosen. Landmark.

items.title: The standard bilinear form $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_{i<n}x_iy_i$ on $F^{n}$
items.strategy: Define $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ on $F^n$ over an arbitrary field and prove it is a symmetric bilinear form in the sense of [[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]], and that it is nondegenerate in the sense of [[def-matrix-radicals-rank-and-nondegeneracy-of-a-bilinear-form]] (its matrix in the standard basis is the identity). SAY EXPLICITLY, IN THE DEFINITION, that this is NOT an inner product unless $F$ is $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ with the published convention: over $\mathbb{F}_2$ there is no order and no positivity, and $\langle x,x\rangle=0$ holds for many nonzero $x$. Record $\langle x,x\rangle=\sum_i x_i$ over $\mathbb{F}_2$, since $t^2=t$ there. Landmark.

items.title: $\langle v_A,v_B\rangle$ is the image of $\lvert A\cap B\rvert$ in $F$; over $\mathbb{F}_2$ it is $0$ or $1$ according to the parity of $\lvert A\cap B\rvert$
items.strategy: Expand the sum: the term at $i$ is $1_F$ when $i\in A\cap B$ and $0_F$ otherwise, so the value is the sum of $\lvert A\cap B\rvert$ copies of $1_F$, which is the image of that natural number under the unique ring map $\mathbb{Z}\to F$. Write it as $\lvert A\cap B\rvert\cdot 1_F$; do not write the canonical embedding applied to a natural number. State the two specialisations used later: over $\mathbb{R}$ the value IS $\lvert A\cap B\rvert$, and over $\mathbb{F}_2$ it is $1$ exactly when $\lvert A\cap B\rvert$ is odd. Taking $B=A$ gives $\langle v_A,v_A\rangle=\lvert A\rvert\cdot 1_F$. Landmark.

items.title: A finite family of subsets of $[n]$ and its incidence matrix over $F$
items.strategy: A **family** here is a finite list $\mathcal{F}=(A_1,\dots,A_m)$ of pairwise distinct subsets of $[n]$; its **incidence matrix** $N(\mathcal{F})\in F^{m\times n}$ has $v_{A_i}$ as its $i$-th row. Record that the $(i,j)$ entry of $N N^{\mathsf{T}}$ is $\langle v_{A_i},v_{A_j}\rangle$, using the matrix product of [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]. Distinctness is part of the definition because every bound below counts SETS, and it is the hypothesis a reader drops.

items.title: If the incidence vectors of $A_1,\dots,A_m\subseteq[n]$ are linearly independent over $F$ then $m\le n$
items.strategy: THE MASTER LEMMA OF THE PAGE, and every theorem below is this lemma with a different independence argument in front of it. The incidence vectors lie in $F^{n}$, which has the standard basis of $n$ elements ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), so $\dim_F F^n=n$ and an independent subset has at most $n$ elements by [[cor-independent-set-is-no-larger-than-a-finite-spanning-set]]. Independence of the LIST gives distinctness of the vectors, hence $m$ distinct elements in the set. State it as a lemma about a family, not about vectors: that is the form that makes the citations below faithful. Landmark.

items.title: Diagonal criterion: if $\langle v_i,w_i\rangle\ne0$ and $\langle v_i,w_j\rangle=0$ for $i\ne j$, then $v_1,\dots,v_m$ are linearly independent
items.strategy: Pair a vanishing combination $\sum_i c_iv_i=0$ with $w_j$ and use bilinearity: every term with $i\ne j$ dies and $c_j\langle v_j,w_j\rangle=0$ forces $c_j=0$ since a field has no zero divisors. State it for an arbitrary bilinear form on an arbitrary $F$-vector space, since the page applies it over $\mathbb{F}_2$ and over $\mathbb{R}$ and to polynomial evaluation pairings. NO POSITIVITY AND NO NONDEGENERACY IS USED — only bilinearity and the diagonal, and the Remark says so, because that is exactly what makes the argument legal over $\mathbb{F}_2$. Landmark.

items.title: Triangular criterion: if $\langle v_i,w_i\rangle\ne0$ and $\langle v_i,w_j\rangle=0$ for $j<i$, then $v_1,\dots,v_m$ are linearly independent
items.strategy: Take a vanishing combination with a nonzero coefficient and let $i$ be LEAST with $c_i\ne0$; pairing with $w_i$ kills every term with index $>i$ by the hypothesis and every term with index $<i$ by minimality, leaving $c_i\langle v_i,w_i\rangle=0$. State the index convention once and use it consistently: the hypothesis is one-sided and the direction matters. This is the criterion the intersection bound below uses, where the diagonal criterion is unavailable.

items.title: Determinant criterion: if the matrix $\bigl(\langle v_i,w_j\rangle\bigr)_{i,j}$ is invertible then both $v_1,\dots,v_m$ and $w_1,\dots,w_m$ are linearly independent
items.strategy: If $\sum_ic_iv_i=0$ then $c^{\mathsf{T}}M=0$ for $M=(\langle v_i,w_j\rangle)$, and invertibility gives $c=0$; symmetrically for the $w_j$. Cite the invertible-matrix theorem of [[thm-invertible-matrix-theorem]] for the equivalence with nonzero determinant. The three criteria are stated separately because every later proof names exactly one of them.

items.title: Oddtown: distinct $A_1,\dots,A_m\subseteq[n]$ with every $\lvert A_i\rvert$ odd and every $\lvert A_i\cap A_j\rvert$ ($i\ne j$) even satisfy $m\le n$
items.strategy: Work over $\mathbb{F}_2$. By [[lem-the-standard-form-of-two-incidence-vectors-is-the-intersection-size]] the hypotheses say $\langle v_{A_i},v_{A_i}\rangle=1$ and $\langle v_{A_i},v_{A_j}\rangle=0$ for $i\ne j$, which is the diagonal criterion with $w_i=v_{A_i}$; then apply [[lem-a-family-with-independent-incidence-vectors-has-at-most-n-members]]. Six numbered steps and no rank-of-a-product theorem. Note in a Remark that the form on $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ is not an inner product and that the argument never needs it to be. Statement from Babai–Frankl §1.1 and Matoušek Miniature 3. Landmark.

items.title: The $n$ singletons form an Oddtown family, so the bound $m\le n$ is attained for every $n$
items.strategy: Check the two hypotheses on $\{\{i\}:i<n\}$: each has size $1$, and distinct singletons meet in the empty set. This is what makes the companion page's false statement ("$n-1$ suffices") refutable in two lines, and it is worth an item because the sharpness is used, not merely mentioned.

items.title: A $d$-dimensional vector space over a field with $q$ elements has exactly $q^{d}$ elements
items.strategy: Coordinates with respect to an ordered basis give a bijection onto $F^{d}$ ([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]), and $\lvert F^{d}\rvert=q^{d}$ by [[thm-cardinality-of-a-set-of-functions]]. Check $d=0$: one element, $q^0=1$. The library has this nowhere and the Eventown bound needs it, so it is built here rather than gestured at.

items.title: For a subspace $U\le F^{n}$, $\dim_F U^{\perp}=n-\dim_F U$, where $U^{\perp}=\{x:\langle x,u\rangle=0\text{ for all }u\in U\}$
items.strategy: Choose a basis $u_1,\dots,u_d$ of $U$ ([[thm-dimension-of-a-linear-subspace]], which supplies it with NO CHOICE PRINCIPLE in finite dimension) and let $\Phi:F^n\to F^{d}$ send $x$ to $(\langle x,u_1\rangle,\dots,\langle x,u_d\rangle)$. Then $\ker\Phi=U^{\perp}$, and the matrix of $\Phi$ has the $u_i$ as its rows, so its rank is $d$ by [[thm-row-rank-equals-column-rank]] and independence of the rows. Rank–nullity ([[thm-rank-nullity]]) finishes. DO NOT USE THE DOUBLE-ANNIHILATOR THEOREM: it is stated under the axiom of choice, and this page spends none. Valid over every field, degenerate cases $U=0$ and $U=F^n$ included.

items.title: Eventown: distinct $A_1,\dots,A_m\subseteq[n]$ with every $\lvert A_i\rvert$ and every $\lvert A_i\cap A_j\rvert$ even satisfy $m\le 2^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$
items.strategy: Let $U\le\mathbb{F}_2^{n}$ be the span of the incidence vectors. By [[lem-the-standard-form-of-two-incidence-vectors-is-the-intersection-size]] all pairwise values AND all diagonal values vanish, so bilinearity gives $\langle u,u'\rangle=0$ for all $u,u'\in U$, i.e. $U\subseteq U^{\perp}$. Then [[lem-the-orthogonal-complement-of-a-subspace-under-the-standard-form]] gives $\dim U\le n-\dim U$, so $\dim U\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor$; the $m$ distinct incidence vectors lie in $U$, and $\lvert U\rvert=2^{\dim U}$ by [[lem-cardinality-of-a-finite-dimensional-space-over-a-finite-field]]. The floor appears because $\dim U$ is an integer; treat $n$ even and $n$ odd as separate numbered steps. Statement from Babai–Frankl §2.3. Landmark.

items.title: An Eventown family that no further set can be added to has exactly $2^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$ members
items.strategy: Let $\mathcal{F}$ be maximal. First show $\mathcal{F}$ is closed under symmetric difference and contains $\varnothing$, by checking the two parity conditions for $A\triangle B$ against $\lvert A\triangle B\rvert=\lvert A\rvert+\lvert B\rvert-2\lvert A\cap B\rvert$ and using maximality; hence $\{v_A:A\in\mathcal{F}\}$ is a subspace $U$ with $U\subseteq U^{\perp}$. Next show maximality forces $U=U^{\perp}\cap H$ where $H=\{x:\langle x,x\rangle=0\}$ is the even-weight subspace, which over $\mathbb{F}_2$ is the hyperplane $\sum_ix_i=0$. Then compute $\dim U=\lfloor n/2\rfloor$, treating $n$ even and $n$ odd separately: the odd case is where the floor is earned and is the step most likely to be skipped. Verify the whole statement at $n=3$ by hand inside the proof or on the companion page.

items.title: If $v_1,\dots,v_m\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ satisfy $\langle v_i,v_j\rangle=t\ge0$ for $i\ne j$ and $\langle v_i,v_i\rangle>t$, they are linearly independent
items.strategy: Expand $0=\bigl\langle\sum_ic_iv_i,\sum_jc_jv_j\bigr\rangle=\sum_i c_i^2(d_i-t)+t\bigl(\sum_ic_i\bigr)^2$ where $d_i=\langle v_i,v_i\rangle$. Both summands are $\ge0$ because $t\ge0$ and $d_i>t$, so both vanish, and $c_i^2(d_i-t)=0$ forces $c_i=0$. State the equivalent matrix form as a second clause — the Gram matrix $tJ+D$ with $D$ diagonal positive is positive definite in the sense of [[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]], hence invertible — since that is how the sources phrase it. POSITIVITY OF $\mathbb{R}$ IS USED HERE AND IS INDISPENSABLE, which is exactly why the companion page's $\mathbb{F}_2$ false statement is false. Landmark.

items.title: Fisher's inequality, nonuniform form: distinct nonempty $A_1,\dots,A_m\subseteq[n]$ with $\lvert A_i\cap A_j\rvert=t$ for all $i\ne j$ satisfy $m\le n$
items.strategy: Two cases, and the first is the one that is skipped. CASE A: some $\lvert A_i\rvert=t$. Then $t\ge1$ (the sets are nonempty and distinct), that $A_i$ is contained in every other set, the differences $A_j\setminus A_i$ for $j\ne i$ are nonempty and pairwise disjoint, so there are at most $n-\lvert A_i\rvert\le n-1$ of them and $m\le n$. CASE B: every $\lvert A_i\rvert>t$. Over $\mathbb{R}$, [[lem-the-standard-form-of-two-incidence-vectors-is-the-intersection-size]] puts the incidence vectors in the hypothesis of [[lem-real-vectors-with-equal-pairwise-products-and-larger-norms-are-independent]], and [[lem-a-family-with-independent-incidence-vectors-has-at-most-n-members]] finishes. Also check $t=0$ and $m=1$. Statement from Babai–Frankl §4.1 and Matoušek Miniature 4. Landmark.

items.title: A $k$-uniform family on $[n]$ with all pairwise intersections of size $t<k$ has at most $n$ members
items.strategy: The uniform case falls into Case B of [[thm-nonuniform-fisher-inequality]] outright, since $\lvert A_i\rvert=k>t$. State it separately because it is the form the design-theoretic literature uses and the form the companion page applies to the seven lines of the Fano plane. Say in a Remark that the design-theoretic reading ($b\ge v$ for a $2$-design) is not stated here, because block designs are not among this page's declared prerequisites.

items.title: A decomposition of a graph's edge set into complete bipartite subgraphs
items.strategy: Given a finite simple graph $G$ ([[def-finite-simple-graph]]), a **complete bipartite decomposition** is a list of pairs $(X_1,Y_1),\dots,(X_m,Y_m)$ of disjoint nonempty subsets of $V(G)$ such that every edge of $G$ lies in exactly one of the sets $\{\{x,y\}:x\in X_k,\,y\in Y_k\}$ and every such pair is an edge. Note that the $X_k\cup Y_k$ need not cover $V(G)$, and that "exactly one" is the disjointness hypothesis Graham–Pollak needs. Cite [[def-standard-complete-bipartite-path-and-cycle-graphs]] for the complete bipartite graph itself so the notion is not re-minted.

items.title: Graham–Pollak: a complete bipartite decomposition of $K_n$ has at least $n-1$ parts
items.strategy: Suppose $m\le n-2$. The homogeneous real system $\sum_{i<n}x_i=0$ together with $\sum_{i\in X_k}x_i=0$ for $k=1,\dots,m$ has $m+1\le n-1<n$ equations in $n$ unknowns, so it has a nonzero solution $a$ by [[cor-rank-criterion-for-consistency]] and [[thm-rref-consistency-and-free-variable-parametrisation]]. Substituting into the identity $\sum_{i<j}x_ix_j=\sum_{k}\bigl(\sum_{i\in X_k}x_i\bigr)\bigl(\sum_{j\in Y_k}x_j\bigr)$ — which holds because each edge is covered exactly once and $X_k\cap Y_k=\varnothing$, and which needs its own numbered step — gives $0$ on the right, while the left equals $\tfrac12\bigl[(\sum_ia_i)^2-\sum_ia_i^2\bigr]=-\tfrac12\sum_ia_i^2<0$. Contradiction. Also record that $n-1$ is attained, by the star decomposition. Statement from Babai–Frankl §1.4 and Matoušek Miniature 8. Landmark.

items.title: Shattering and the Vapnik–Chervonenkis dimension of a set family
items.strategy: For $\mathcal{F}\subseteq\mathcal{P}([n])$ and $T\subseteq[n]$, the **trace** of $\mathcal{F}$ on $T$ is $\mathcal{F}\vert_T=\{F\cap T:F\in\mathcal{F}\}$, and $\mathcal{F}$ **shatters** $T$ when $\mathcal{F}\vert_T=\mathcal{P}(T)$. The **VC dimension** is the greatest $d$ such that some $T$ with $\lvert T\rvert=d$ is shattered. WELL-DEFINEDNESS IS AN OBLIGATION, not a remark: the empty set is shattered by any nonempty $\mathcal{F}$, the shattered sets are subsets of the finite $[n]$, so the maximum exists by [[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]]; and record the boundary $\operatorname{VC}(\mathcal{F})=0$ for a one-element family and the convention for $\mathcal{F}=\varnothing$. Landmark.

items.title: The down-shift $S_j$ of a set family at a point $j$
items.strategy: For $j<n$ define $S_j(\mathcal{F})=\{s_j(F,\mathcal{F}):F\in\mathcal{F}\}$ where $s_j(F,\mathcal{F})=F\setminus\{j\}$ if $j\in F$ and $F\setminus\{j\}\notin\mathcal{F}$, and $s_j(F,\mathcal{F})=F$ otherwise. Prove immediately that $s_j(\cdot,\mathcal{F})$ is injective on $\mathcal{F}$, so $\lvert S_j(\mathcal{F})\rvert=\lvert\mathcal{F}\rvert$; and define the weight $w(\mathcal{F})=\sum_{F\in\mathcal{F}}\lvert F\rvert$, which is what the termination argument decreases.

items.title: $\lvert S_j(\mathcal{F})\rvert=\lvert\mathcal{F}\rvert$, and $w(S_j(\mathcal{F}))\le w(\mathcal{F})$ with equality only when $S_j(\mathcal{F})=\mathcal{F}$
items.strategy: Injectivity of $s_j$: if $s_j(F)=s_j(G)$ with $F\ne G$ then one of them was shifted and the other not, and unwinding the two clauses gives a contradiction — write out the case split rather than asserting it. The weight claim is immediate from the definition. THIS AND THE NEXT LEMMA ARE SEPARATE ITEMS ON PURPOSE: Sauer–Shelah by shifting is unprovable without both, and running them together is how the argument is usually left incomplete.

items.title: Every set shattered by $S_j(\mathcal{F})$ is shattered by $\mathcal{F}$
items.strategy: Let $T$ be shattered by $\mathcal{G}=S_j(\mathcal{F})$. If $j\notin T$ the trace on $T$ only shrinks, and one checks $\mathcal{G}\vert_T\subseteq\mathcal{F}\vert_T$ directly. If $j\in T$, take $A\subseteq T$; both $A$ and $A\cup\{j\}$ are traces of $\mathcal{G}$, and the definition of $s_j$ forces the corresponding pair of members of $\mathcal{F}$ to realise $A$ and $A\cup\{j\}$ as well. Each case is a numbered step, and the case $j\in T$ is where the "and $F\setminus\{j\}\notin\mathcal{F}$" clause of the shift is used.

items.title: Applying down-shifts until none changes the family terminates, and the result is closed under taking subsets
items.strategy: Termination: each effective shift strictly decreases the natural number $w(\mathcal{F})$ of [[def-down-shift-of-a-set-family]], so there is no infinite descending chain. Downward closure of a fixed family: if $S_j(\mathcal{F})=\mathcal{F}$ for every $j$, then $F\in\mathcal{F}$ and $j\in F$ imply $F\setminus\{j\}\in\mathcal{F}$, and induction on $\lvert F\setminus G\rvert$ gives $G\in\mathcal{F}$ for every $G\subseteq F$.

items.title: If $\mathcal{F}$ is closed under taking subsets then $\mathcal{F}$ shatters every $F\in\mathcal{F}$
items.strategy: For $A\subseteq F$ we have $A\in\mathcal{F}$ and $A\cap F=A$, so $\mathcal{F}\vert_F=\mathcal{P}(F)$. Two lines, but it is the step that converts a structural fact into a size bound.

items.title: Sauer–Shelah: a family on $[n]$ of VC dimension at most $d$ has at most $\sum_{i=0}^{d}\binom{n}{i}$ members
items.strategy: Shift $\mathcal{F}$ to a fixed family $\mathcal{G}$ by [[lem-iterated-down-shifting-terminates-in-a-downward-closed-family]]. Then $\lvert\mathcal{G}\rvert=\lvert\mathcal{F}\rvert$ by [[lem-the-down-shift-preserves-the-number-of-sets]] and $\operatorname{VC}(\mathcal{G})\le d$ by [[lem-the-down-shift-creates-no-new-shattered-set]]; $\mathcal{G}$ is downward closed, so by [[lem-a-downward-closed-family-shatters-each-of-its-members]] every $G\in\mathcal{G}$ has $\lvert G\rvert\le d$, and the sets of size at most $d$ number $\sum_{i\le d}\binom{n}{i}$ by [[def-binomial-coefficient]] and [[thm-sum-rule]]. Check $d=0$ and $d=n$. Landmark.

items.title: For $d\ge1$ a family on $[n]$ of VC dimension at most $d$ has at most $(n+1)^{d}$ members
items.strategy: Bound $\binom{n}{i}\le n^{i}$ from [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]], then $\sum_{i=0}^{d}n^{i}\le(n+1)^{d}$ by the binomial theorem, since $(n+1)^d=\sum_j\binom{d}{j}n^j$ and $\binom{d}{j}\ge1$ for $0\le j\le d$. STATE THE HYPOTHESIS $d\ge1$ AND CHECK $n=0$ AND $n=1$: the companion page's false statement is the same bound with $n^{d}$ in place of $(n+1)^{d}$, which fails at small $n$, so the two must not be confused.

items.title: The inclusion matrix $W_{t,k}(n)$ of $t$-sets against $k$-sets
items.strategy: For $t\le k\le n$ let $W_{t,k}(n)$ be the matrix over $\mathbb{Q}$ whose rows are indexed by the $t$-element subsets of $[n]$, whose columns are indexed by the $k$-element subsets, and whose $(S,K)$ entry is $1$ when $S\subseteq K$ and $0$ otherwise; fix an ordering of the index sets once so the matrix is well defined up to simultaneous permutation, and say that its rank does not depend on that choice. Record $W_{t,t}(n)=I$ and $W_{0,k}(n)$ = the all-ones row. Also record the composition identity $W_{s,t}(n)\,W_{t,k}(n)=\binom{k-s}{t-s}W_{s,k}(n)$ for $s\le t\le k$, proved by counting the $t$-sets between a fixed $s$-set and a fixed $k$-set; that count is $\binom{k-s}{t-s}$ when $S\subseteq K$ and $0$ otherwise. Landmark.

items.title: $\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb{Q}}W_{1,k}(n)=n$ for $1\le k\le n-1$
items.strategy: Suppose $\sum_{i<n}c_i[i\in K]=0$ for every $k$-set $K$, that is $\sum_{i\in K}c_i=0$ for every $k$-set $K$. For $i\ne j$ pick a $k$-set $K$ containing $i$ but not $j$ — possible exactly because $1\le k\le n-1$ — and swap $i$ for $j$; subtracting the two equations gives $c_i=c_j$. Hence all $c_i$ are equal to some $c$, and $kc=0$ with $k\ge1$ gives $c=0$ in $\mathbb{Q}$. So the rows are independent and the rank is $n$. STATE THE RANGE AND SHOW BOTH ENDS FAIL: at $k=n$ the single column makes the rank $1$, and at $k=0$ there are no rows to speak of. This is the case the companion page computes; the general rank formula is a separate matter recorded in the next remark.

items.title: What is and is not proved about $\operatorname{rank}W_{t,k}(n)$ on this page
items.strategy: Say exactly what the page establishes — the composition identity and the case $t=1$ — and what it does not: the theorem that $\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb{Q}}W_{t,k}(n)=\binom{n}{t}$ whenever $t\le k\le n-t$.
